 View Comments Rose Marie Wagner, a member of the Harvard Academic Workers Union, uses a bullhorn during a demonstration Tuesday at Harvard University. David L. Ryan/Globe Staff Hundreds of academic workers at Harvard University joined graduate students on the picket line Tuesday, walking off the job in an attempt to bring the academic arm of the university to a halt as economic and political pressures continue to drive bargaining negotiations. 
 The Harvard Academic Workers Union — which represents researchers and nontenure track faculty — is the second union to go on strike in recent weeks , joining the graduate student union which has been on strike since Oct. 28. Roughly 6,500 members are eligible to strike between the two unions. 
 Related : Stephen Colbert, Yo-Yo Ma event at Harvard cut short by fire alarm as demonstrators chant outside The addition of academic workers continues to impact classroom instruction, as teachers for some of the university’s required courses and lab sessions have walked off the job. Members of both unions circled the Science Center Plaza outside Harvard Yard, with chants of “Harvard messed up, now we’re two.” 
 The Harvard Academic Workers Union joined the Harvard Graduate Students Union on the picket line Tuesday at the university's Science Center Plaza. David L. Ryan/Globe Staff Dining workers could be the third union to join the picket line, after they voted to authorize a strike last month. The law school clinicians union is also currently in bargaining talks with the administration, but have not indicated that they will strike yet. 
 This is the first time the academic workers group has negotiated a contract with Harvard after they formed a union in April 2024. Bargaining talks have spanned two years and more than 50 sessions. 
 Many tenets of the dual strikes are in unison: calls for higher pay, stronger policies against harassment and discrimination, and protections for those at Harvard on international visas. 
 But for the academic workers, union members assert the university has stalled talks for them to build their foundational contract. The academic workers and Harvard have reached an agreement on 27 articles, but remain at an impasse over compensation, workplace protections, and definitions of who is eligible to join the union. 
 Harvard disagrees. In a letter sent to the community ahead of the strike, John Manning, Harvard’s provost, and Meredith Weenick, the executive vice president, said the university has offered wage increases and already agreed to several union priorities, including eliminating a longstanding “time cap” policy that meant some instructors were not eligible to continue their roles after a certain number of years. 
 “While negotiating an initial contract requires significant time due to the absence of pre-existing language from which to work, the two parties have made substantial progress on many issues and topic areas,” Manning and Weenick wrote. 
 Over the last two weeks, graduate students have shouted calls not to cross the picket line, disrupting guest speakers on campus. Some professors have said loud rallies outside classrooms have distracted students inside sitting for exams. 
 Harvard workers go on strike on Tuesday. David L. Ryan/Globe Staff On Tuesday, first-year students enrolled in a required expository writing course, got an email with instructions to complete online modules in lieu of class, if needed. Many of the faculty who teach this class are in the academic workers union. 
 Ian Shank, one of the writing teachers, said to walk away from his classes “hurts.” But since the union formed two years ago, he said his pay has stayed stagnant while his class sizes have increased. 
 “We’re not asking for the moon,” said Shank, who makes roughly $75,000 a year. “Over the last few years it has become harder to do my job.” 
 Maxuel Tavarez Marcelino, a freshman student in expository writing, spotted his teacher in the picket line, as the unions marched through Harvard Yard among other people walking between classes and tourists stopping for selfies with the John Harvard statue. 
 A drum circle in took shape in the middle of the yard as the parade of protesters circled through the gates before reconvening on the plaza, where a makeshift hub has been set up for union members — with plastic tables, wagons of signs, snacks, and spare bullhorns. 
 Tavarez Marcelino understands why his teachers are on strike, he said, and anticipated that grading would now be at a standstill and sections for larger discussions would also not meet. But he doesn’t blame the faculty. 
 “It’s more frustration with the administration,” Tavarez Marcelino said. “You have all this money and you can’t stand besides your workers. It’s an embarrassment.” 
 Repeated chants on the picket line have ridiculed the university’s growing endowment, which reached $68 billion, according to financial reports released last month. But the university asserts the majority of the money is restricted — meaning that it must be spent toward a purpose designated by donors — and not immediately accessible. 
 But the disparity between what the university embodies — it is the wealthiest institution in the world — and what it pays its employees, is hard to grasp for longtime employees like Chip Robinson, who teaches German and Old Icelandic languages, and previously worked at Harvard as a librarian for 15 years. 
 His return to Harvard five years ago, as a nontenured faculty member, has come with worse working conditions, he said. 
 With his students, Robinson enjoys advising them on their senior theses, writing recommendation letters, and working closely together in class. But as an instructor, he feels his job does not come with any protections. He has watched as other faculty are let go weeks into the semester, due to low enrollment in courses. 
 “There’s no reasonable insurance of re-employment,” he said. “We all know how endowed funds work but the return on investment for the university is beyond all proportion. They always have money for buildings and administration and landscaping.” 
 The academic workers strike includes teaching and research staff across the arts and sciences, engineer, divinity, and medical school. Kelsey Tyssowski, a postdoc in the biology department, decided to pause her research to go on strike. It’s not an easy decision, she said — she uses mice for her studies — “but I just feel like we are in a position where the things that we are asking for seem very reasonable.” 
 “People are in incredibly precarious positions. You’re not paid enough. Some people here do not have health insurance,” she said. “They work here full time.” 
 Shadows are cast by Harvard workers going on strike. David L. Ryan/Globe Staff When Budom Ezeani, a freshman, visited Harvard last year for admitted students day, the graduate students were in the middle of their previous 40-day strike, which paused as the school year ended. 
 Now, he has watched the picket line resume from his dorm window, which overlooks Harvard Yard, and grow with the addition of the academic workers. 
 “I’m pretty proud,” he said. “This is the first step to a lot of positive change at this school.”
